packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, in part because it also reduced autopay enrollment and increased missed payments among liquidity-constrained cardholders.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment with six-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows that changing enrollment defaults for a liquid, self-directed consumer financial product can shift nominal enrollment behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome, and can even backfire via missed payments among liquidity-constrained users — directly bears on whether opt-out enrollment in round-up savings will produce real savings or just nominal sign-ups.
limitations: about credit card debt repayment, not savings accumulation
abstract gives no effect size on debt itself, only on payment behavior
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests a consumer financial nudge/default change with liquidity-constrained users and shows enrollment change decoupled from the real outcome — closest empirical analog to the round-up decision.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: In experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default options for risky-asset allocation produce medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but implementing a default nudge (especially one the client would refuse) lowers the client's rating of the wealth manager's advice, with framing of the default question also shifting allocations.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative-sample experiment across five European countries testing default nudges and framing in investment decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial default reads as manipulative versus helpful in a European consumer-facing advisory context, showing defaults can damage trust — this is the exact dark-pattern/reputational risk the brief flags for our EU product, and cautions against a one-size-fits-all preset multiplier.
limitations: investment/wealth management context rather than a savings round-up feature
no follow-up beyond the initial decision, so persistence unmeasured
packets.relevance_reason: European, consumer-facing financial-decision experiment directly measuring when a default is perceived as manipulative, exactly the reputational risk question the brief raises.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites raised donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple 2020 US campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring-donation boxes at different times.
packets.why_it_matters: A near-perfect consumer-digital analogue to a pre-checked enrollment default: it shows a default can raise nominal sign-ups while generating complaints/refunds and disproportionately affecting inexperienced users, mirroring the support team's exact worry about the round-up feature.
limitations: political donations rather than personal savings
refund/complaint outcome is a proxy for disengagement, not a direct engagement or withdrawal measure
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests default effects on amount and heterogeneity in a self-directed consumer digital-payment setting close to the brief's own concerns.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation, and only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later — sets the ceiling our default-design decision should be measured against.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives 401(k)-specific figures that may not map onto round-up savings
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving amounts long-term, which the brief asked us to look for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Mandated browser choice screens under the EU Digital Markets Act raised Firefox usage 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting from 15 months after rollout onward.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences analysis around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen mandate across iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: Real-world evidence that a regulator-mandated active choice screen produces large, persistent behavior change in a mobile app setting under EU law — the closest available test of whether active choice meaningfully counters entrenched defaults in exactly our regulatory and device context.
limitations: browser selection, not a financial savings decision
no measure of user-reported satisfaction, complaints, or disengagement
packets.relevance_reason: Directly evidences the persistence and magnitude of active-choice effects in a mobile app, EU-regulated context, bearing on decision 1.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million annually, though alerts still leave more than half of avoidable overdrafts unaddressed.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run by major UK retail banks on live customer accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: This is a consumer banking automatic-enrollment result, not a pension analogy: it shows defaults can move real financial behavior at scale in exactly our setting, while also showing a persistent gap between potential and realized benefit that supports the support team's disengagement concern.
limitations: measures charge avoidance, not savings amounts or a round-up product specifically
no explicit 6-12 month retention/withdrawal analysis
packets.relevance_reason: The closest available consumer-banking automatic-enrollment evidence with real effect sizes, directly bearing on the entry decision.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for downstream (later-in-time) effects of choice-architecture defaults on consumer behavior, identifying time course, prior preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist.
packets.methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing prior findings into a framework and research agenda. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to think about exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief raises — which downstream outcomes to measure and what moderates whether a default's effect on enrollment translates into lasting engagement.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not new empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: Directly addresses how and when default effects persist or fade over time in consumer settings, the core uncertainty the brief flags about vanity enrollment.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges including default options significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default nudges.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: A direct empirical contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, in a self-directed voluntary-savings decision context with reported heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
limitations: voluntary pension saving in China, cultural/institutional context may differ from EU consumer banking
online survey stated intentions rather than live product enrollment or actual money
packets.relevance_reason: Directly requested by the brief: a study contradicting the assumption that defaults reliably raise saving, with distributional detail on who is helped or hurt.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: Synthesizes the behavioural household finance literature across savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance, and reviews interventions including choice architecture, product design, and disclosure that firms and governments use to shape financial behaviour.
packets.methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter (NBER), abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the broad map of which choice-architecture levers (defaults, product design, disclosure) have evidence behind them in consumer finance generally, useful for sanity-checking that our two design decisions are the right ones to focus scarce evidence-gathering on.
limitations: broad narrative review without a systematic protocol
abstract does not give effect sizes specific to round-up savings or active choice
covers household finance broadly rather than fintech-app enrolment specifically
packets.relevance_reason: The review/synthesis anchor giving a landscape of behavioural household-finance interventions, the kind of overview the brief asks for alongside single-study evidence.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment with a financial-management platform found payment reminders cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated in users with an overdraft history, who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment on a consumer financial-management platform in Brazil comparing reminder vs. no-reminder groups, tracking downstream fee outcomes across products.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users on average while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the heterogeneity risk the brief says we must check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft context rather than round-up savings
no long-horizon (6-12 month) persistence data reported in abstract
packets.relevance_reason: Best available evidence in a consumer financial self-directed setting for the brief's explicit worry about who is helped versus hurt by nudge-style interventions.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — a forced-choice design that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as an alternative to automatic enrolment that can nudge behaviour without a default.
alternates.methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature plus two original field experiments testing standard active choice vs. enhanced (loss-framed) active choice against no intervention.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, testable design for the active-choice arm of the entry decision: forcing a yes/no answer while loss-framing the 'no round-up' option could capture much of the opt-out enrolment benefit without the disengagement risk of true auto-enrolment.
limitations: field experiments are in medication adherence, not financial savings
does not report enrolment persistence or amount saved at 6-12 months
no direct test in a consumer banking or fintech context
alternates.relevance_reason: The specific mechanism transfers directly to the entry-design decision: 'enhanced active choice' is a concrete alternative to opt-out that the brief's active-choice question is asking about.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: An opt-in short-term, liquid, withdraw-anytime payroll savings program at five UK firms saw very low take-up (at most 0.7% of eligible employees activated an account), but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
alternates.methodology: Field study of program introduction and administrative account data over the first 12 months, five UK firms.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly answers the opt-in persistence question for a liquid short-term savings product, our closest real-world analog: opt-in take-up is very low, but retention among opt-ins is very high, suggesting opt-in enrollment may not be a vanity metric once someone actually signs up, though it also confirms the low-enrollment cost of pure opt-in.
limitations: payroll-deduction employer channel, so the employer-as-intermediary mechanism may partly drive take-up and cannot be fully separated from product design
does not report amounts saved beyond having a positive balance
alternates.relevance_reason: The closest empirical analog to the product being built — a liquid, withdraw-anytime, opt-in savings account — giving concrete opt-in take-up and 12-month retention figures.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people rate financial nudges positively overall, prefer System 2 (deliberative) interventions and savings-framed messaging over spending-framed messaging, and transparency has no significant effect on approval.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment with 36 hypothetical scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; six dependent variables including approval and perceived manipulation.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly informs how to frame and communicate the round-up enrolment choice (savings framing preferred, System 2/deliberate framing preferred) to avoid a dark-pattern reputational risk, and shows disclosure of mechanism need not hurt approval.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual product behaviour
Australian sample, not EU
does not measure enrolment or persistence outcomes
alternates.relevance_reason: Speaks directly to whether a default or nudge reads as helpful vs manipulative, the EU reputational-risk question the brief raises.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable dark patterns under existing EU law.
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis mapping EU statutes onto a normative autonomy framework; abstract-only, no empirical data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the team a defensible EU legal test for whether an opt-out default (pre-selected enrollment or pre-selected multiplier) crosses from helpful default into a regulable dark pattern, directly informing how entry and level are framed and disclosed.
limitations: purely doctrinal/legal, no behavioral effect sizes
not specific to financial products or savings features
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation risk the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the opt-out design.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus ~50% at lower defaults), and non-opters clustered at the suboptimal default rather than choosing higher matched contributions.
alternates.methodology: Administrative data analysis of a single employer retirement plan with a high default rate; includes a literature review of opt-out rates at lower defaults.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly evidences that a pre-set level anchors people at a fixed point even when it is suboptimal for them, which is the exact risk the brief raises about defaulting the round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer product
the trusted-employer-intermediary mechanism the brief says does not carry over
alternates.relevance_reason: Strong anchoring evidence for decision 2, but capped for being an employer-plan setting rather than consumer self-directed.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making.
